touches.text: Reds don't get lost. Each run writes a ticket for every new red it finds and every orphaned file it sees, unless one is already open for it. A red seen in passing gets the same treatment. Every red and every orphaned file is fixed; one unrelated to the work in hand is ticketed, and once it is, that crossing can go ahead.
Test tiers: commit, hourly, daily and weekly. Each tier runs only what it must, so a commit needs only its own proofs and the long runs wait for the long tiers; nothing runs just in case.

A retirement checks its callers in the same act as the deletion: nothing imports the module being deleted, and nothing runs the command or path being deleted. A file that only names it (a fixture, a record, a charter) is not a caller. Nothing checks afterwards. Why? Naming is history; only a caller breaks, and a caller that comes later breaks loudly on its own. A standing proof that a thing stays gone is history kept as code.
Code that is no longer needed is deleted. Git history keeps it if we ever need it back.

These files live in cairn/devices/cairn/requirements/, one per section, and TOC.md names each. They are the map of the system; there is no other. Git keeps every version. Why? EVIDENCE: Because we tried 'the intentions with the code' and that didn't work.

Every line has an outline number; refer to anything by it ("5.5.3"). Lines are renumbered after each round of edits, so a number holds within one conversation, not across them. Why? Because we can refer to those numbers in the chats. -amm
